title: Why is it a "murder" of crows? | COLLECTIVE NOUNS

entries.note: The episode's topic: words for groups of animals or people, also called [[see:nouns of assembly]] or [[see:terms of venery]], many from the 15th-century [[see:Book of St Albans]].
Another name for [[see:collective noun]]s.
Another name for [[see:collective noun]]s, from [[from:venery]], the sport of hunting.
The sport of hunting, from Latin [[from:venari]], to chase or pursue; since the 15th century also a double entendre for sexual pursuits.
Rob recalls this term when finding the sexual sense of [[see:venery]].
Refers to crows' long association with death in legend and folklore; revived in the 19th and 20th centuries; prompts the [[see:attempted murder]] joke.
One of the old collective nouns revived in later centuries and still used.
Not in the original books; a listener from Namibia told Rob it is genuinely used there.
Given as a familiar everyday collective noun.
Seems ordinary but is as coded as the others, alluding to the lion's association with the sin of pride, as in [[see:medieval bestiaries]].
Listed as one of the more fun collective nouns.
Surprisingly old; the hosts link it to [[same-root:flamboyant]] and [[same-root:flamingo]], both meaning flaming.
Listed as one of the more fun collective nouns.
Listed as one of the more fun collective nouns.
A collective noun Rob wouldn't expect to date from the 15th century.
Books linking mythology and morality to animals, with oddly drawn human-faced lions; Jess suspects overlap with the [[see:Book of St Albans]].
Predates Lewis Carroll; possibly from cat-shaped Cheshire cheeses, a tavern sign with a grinning lion, or cats grinning at the county's abundant milk.
Late 15th-century courtesy book on hawking, hunting and [[see:blazing of arms]], partly in rhyme, listing 162 collective nouns; attributed perhaps to [[see:Juliana Berners]].
Refers to the symbols on coats of arms, illustrated at length in the [[see:Book of St Albans]].
A nun, probably a gentleman's daughter, who wrote treatises on hawking and hunting; historians dispute whether she wrote the [[see:Book of St Albans]].
A fashionable late-medieval genre teaching aspiring people how to behave at court, like the [[see:Book of St Albans]] and [[see:The Complete Gentleman]].
An example of a [[see:courtesy book]], subtitled about fashioning a noble gentleman absolute in qualities of mind and body.
A concept imported later from France, about deliberately distinct courtly behaviours that marked who belonged.
Collective term for baby animals, alluding to a dog giving birth on a straw floor.

entries.term: The Companies of Beasties and Fowls
entries.note: The section of the [[see:Book of St Albans]] listing collective nouns; hard to read due to unstandardised spelling and odd letterforms.
From the rhyming verse in the [[see:Book of St Albans]] instructing readers which group words to use.
From the rhyming verse in the [[see:Book of St Albans]].
From the rhyming verse in the [[see:Book of St Albans]].
From the [[see:Book of St Albans]] verse; its spelling there shows how it was pronounced.
A general term for birds, which make up much of the book's list.
One of the many bird terms in the [[see:Book of St Albans]].
Because nightingales sit whistling in trees, watching passers-by.
Coots apparently hide away, though Rob finds them conspicuous.
One of the bird terms in the [[see:Book of St Albans]].
From the [[see:Book of St Albans]], which also uses gaggle for ladies.
One of the book's collective nouns for people rather than animals.
One of the book's collective nouns for people.
One of the book's collective nouns for people.
One of the book's collective nouns for people.
Jess's favourite, amusing since [[see:Juliana Berners]] was herself a nun.
Reflects the religious context and social commentary embedded in the book's terms.
Another socially pointed term from the book.
From the book; prompts discussion of [[see:bevy]].
Rare in British English but common in American business speak; Rob found an American script's "bevy of laws" odd.
Fits the book's purpose of warning readers about the perils of courtly life.
Like [[see:murder of crows]], reflects ravens' folkloric association with death.
Implies [[see:busyness]]; ferret owners call even two ferrets a business; also called a [[see:fesnyng of ferrets]] from the book's spelling.
The state of being busy, distinguished in Middle English from business as an occupation; played on in [[see:business of ferrets]].
Rob's close-second favourite, clearly ironic; hard to decipher because the book's w looks like a b.
Punchline to the joke about a single crow, playing on [[see:murder of crows]].
Via French flamboyant, flaming or wavy, a 15th-century architectural style with flame-like curves; shares a root with [[same-root:flamingo]].
Means flame-coloured bird, when pink counted as a shade of red; shares a root with [[same-root:flamboyant]].
The French name specifies the colour, like English [[equivalent:pink flamingo]].
Used in English for at least one flamingo species, like French [[equivalent:flamant rose]].
An old term revived in later centuries; one of Jess's favourites.
In the [[see:Book of St Albans]] but rarely heard; uses an old sense of [[see:sleuth]].
In the 12th century meant to track or trail, hence a detective on a criminal's trail; unrelated to [[unrelated:sloth]].
An early variant of [[see:sleuth]], unrelated to the animal name.
An 1800s word for a [[see:bloodhound]], which the hosts prefer.
Compared with [[see:sleuth hound]]; the hosts find the word harrowing for such a floppy dog.
Not in the book because [[see:shark]] then referred to a person, not an animal.
In the 1400s a scoundrel or swindler, probably from a German word for villain; extended to the fish around the 16th century.
With card sharp, an example of the original human sense of [[see:shark]].
An example of the original human sense of [[see:shark]].
One of the separate names once given to kinds of [[see:shark]], still used for certain species.
Naval slang for a [[see:shark]] that Rob came across.
Jess's suggested alternative to [[see:crash of rhinos]].
An unofficial collective noun Rob likes.
An alternative to [[see:huddle of walruses]].
An unofficial collective noun Rob calls very elegant.
Evokes a quiver of arrows, as if carrying snakes on your back.
Suggests its coiners weren't fans of cats; the courtesy-book term was [[see:clowder]].
The courtesy books' collective noun for cats, a variation on [[from:clutter]].
Perhaps from elephants as performers, or because they walk in a line.
Used for sheep, goats, birds and Christians; Old English flocc, perhaps from Old Norse [[from?:flokkr]] brought by the Vikings.
Old English with Germanic cognates; may refer to movement, relating it to [[same-root?:swerve]], or be imitative of sound.
Possibly related to [[same-root?:swarm]] if that word refers to movement.
A collective noun the hosts invent for their own occupation.
An invented collective noun the hosts think should be official.
Jess likes it because wombats seem wise and ponderous.
From the [[see:Book of St Albans]], evoking cobblers drinking together and making [[see:shoddy]] shoes.
Originally offcuts of cloth reworked into new cloth, a weaving term, perhaps a variation on [[from?:shed]].
A collective noun of uncertain officialness Jess has seen in several places.
One of Jess's favourite collective nouns.
A collective noun that makes Rob titter.
Alternative to [[see:business of ferrets]], arising because business in the [[see:Book of St Albans]] looks spelled this way in early print.
